brain.name: Brain & Mind
brain.fn: Thinking, reaction speed, mood and sleep. It is very sensitive to CO₂, tiredness and isolation.
brain.effect: In weightlessness body fluids shift toward the head, which can cause headaches and raise pressure inside the skull. A small cabin can let CO₂ build up. Long confinement disturbs sleep and mood. Deep-space radiation is a long-term risk for the nervous system.
brain.why: Slower reactions and poor sleep show up before you feel impaired — catching them early prevents mistakes during EVAs, docking or repairs.

eyes.name: Eyes & Vision
eyes.fn: Focus light and send images to the brain through the optic nerve.
eyes.effect: Fluid shift can swell the optic nerve and flatten the back of the eyeball (Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome, SANS), making near vision blurry or farsighted. Radiation raises long-term cataract risk.
eyes.why: Vision change is gradual and easy to miss. A regular quick test lets the flight surgeon see a trend and plan imaging or glasses.

heart.name: Heart & Circulation
heart.fn: Pumps blood to the whole body and keeps blood pressure stable.
heart.effect: Without gravity about 2 litres of fluid move toward the chest and head, the heart works less and gets deconditioned, and standing up after landing or on a planet can cause fainting.
heart.why: Resting heart rate and blood pressure are the fastest check of circulation, dehydration, stress and illness.

lungs.name: Lungs & Breathing
lungs.fn: Bring oxygen into the blood and remove CO₂.
lungs.effect: Cabin air can have high CO₂, smoke or dust. On the Moon and Mars fine dust is irritating to the airways. In weightlessness gas exchange in the lungs is distributed differently, but oxygen levels normally stay stable.
lungs.why: Blood oxygen (SpO₂) and breathing rate quickly reveal air-quality problems, infection or fire/smoke exposure.

gut.name: Metabolism & Hydration
gut.fn: Digestion, energy (blood sugar), water balance and body mass.
gut.effect: Astronauts often eat and drink less in space, lose body fluid, and can lose weight. Fluid shifts and low hydration raise kidney-stone risk. Stress and altered routines can change blood sugar.
gut.why: Simple checks of blood glucose, urine colour and body mass show whether food and water intake match your needs.

msk.name: Bones & Muscles
msk.fn: Support the body, allow movement and store calcium.
msk.effect: Without normal loading, bones lose roughly 1–2% of density per month in the hips and spine and muscles shrink. The spine lengthens, which often causes back pain. Exercise (resistive + aerobic) is the main countermeasure.
msk.why: Bone loss is silent. Tracking daily exercise and back pain tells you whether your countermeasures are enough.

immune.name: Whole body: Immunity, Skin & Radiation
immune.fn: Defends against infection and tracks overall condition and radiation exposure.
immune.effect: Spaceflight stress and microgravity change immune function and can wake up dormant viruses. Radiation exposure is higher than on Earth and can spike during solar particle events.
immune.why: Temperature is the first sign of infection; the personal dosimeter shows when to take shelter and how much dose you have accumulated.

iss.name: Space station (low Earth orbit)
iss.esc: Ground contact is near real-time — request a private medical conference with the flight surgeon.

notes.msk: Pure weightlessness: no natural loading — full exercise routine every day.

orion.name: Spacecraft (cislunar, Orion-class)
orion.esc: About 3 s delay — call the flight surgeon and stabilise the crew member while you talk.

notes.lungs: Very small cabin: CO₂ rises quickly if ventilation is blocked — check CO₂ first for headaches.
notes.brain: Outside Earth's magnetic field radiation is higher than on the station.

moon.name: Lunar base (south pole)
moon.esc: About 3 s delay — contact the flight surgeon; stabilise first, then follow the remote advice.

notes.lungs: Lunar dust is sharp and irritating — rinse eyes, wear masks, keep suits out of living areas.
notes.eyes: Lunar dust can scratch eyes: use protective eyewear and report irritation.
notes.msk: 0.16 g gives some loading but far from enough — keep resistive exercise.

mars.name: Mars surface base
mars.esc: Round-trip delay is 8–44 minutes: START the onboard medical protocol now, then send data and a message to the flight surgeon and wait for the reply.

notes.lungs: Martian dust contains toxic perchlorates — avoid dust exposure indoors.
notes.msk: 0.38 g helps, yet bone and muscle still need regular resistive exercise.
notes.brain: Isolation and 20-min delays make stress and sleep tracking especially important.

transit.name: Mars transit spacecraft
transit.esc: Delay can reach ~44 min: START the onboard medical protocol now, then send data to the flight surgeon and wait for the reply.

notes.brain: Radiation is highest on the way to Mars, and isolation is longest.
notes.msk: Months of weightlessness — protect bones and muscles with daily exercise.

INDS.name: Headache intensity
INDS.why: Fluid shifts to the head and high cabin CO₂ both cause headaches. A new or worsening headache can be the first sign of CO₂ build-up.
how: Think of the worst headache you had since yesterday.
Rate it: 0 = none, 10 = worst imaginable.
Note nausea, vision changes or confusion.
a1: Drink water and rest.
Check the cabin CO₂ reading and ventilation.
Re-check in 1 hour.
a2: Check CO₂ now and move to a well-ventilated area.
Report to the crew medical officer — especially with vomiting, confusion or vision change.

INDS.name: Reaction time (PVT)
INDS.why: The Psychomotor Vigilance Test measures alertness. Tiredness slows reactions before you feel impaired.
how: Sit still and remove distractions.
Press the circle as soon as it turns green (5 trials).
Use the game button — it fills the value for you.
a1: You may be fatigued: plan rest or a nap.
Avoid risky tasks until you re-test.
Review sleep, caffeine and workload.
a2: Significant impairment: do not perform safety-critical tasks alone.
Ask a crewmate to double-check your work and tell the flight surgeon.

INDS.name: Sleep last night
INDS.why: Astronauts often sleep only ~6 h in orbit. Chronic sleep loss hurts memory, mood, immunity and reaction time.
how: Check your sleep tracker or estimate time actually asleep.
Enter total hours slept.
a1: Protect sleep time: dim lights, reduce noise, consistent bedtime.
Limit caffeine in the 6 h before bed.
a2: Severe sleep loss: ask the flight surgeon about schedule changes or sleep aids.
Avoid critical operations while exhausted.

INDS.name: Stress / mood
INDS.why: Isolation, confinement and workload strain mental health. Tracking mood shows trends early.
how: 0 = calm and fine, 10 = overwhelmed.
Be honest — this is for you and your care team.
a1: Take a break, talk to a crewmate or family (private conference).
Do a breathing exercise or exercise session.
a2: Persistent high stress: schedule a private conference with the behavioural-health support team.

INDS.name: Near-vision blur
INDS.why: Spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) can blur near vision during long missions.
how: Hold printed text at ~40 cm (arm bent).
Cover one eye and read the smallest print; repeat with the other eye.
Rate blur: 0 = sharp, 10 = cannot read normal text.
a1: Repeat in a few days and keep the trend.
Mention it at the next medical conference.
Reading glasses may help — ask the flight surgeon.
a2: Report at once — especially sudden loss, flashes or missing areas.
The flight surgeon may request eye imaging.

INDS.name: Resting heart rate
INDS.why: Resting heart rate rises with dehydration, fever, stress or poor fitness.
how: Rest quietly for 5 minutes.
Use a pulse oximeter or watch, or count pulse at the wrist for 30 s and double.
Measure at the same time each day.
a1: Drink fluid, rest and re-measure in 30 min.
Check temperature and stress level.
a2: Persistent very high or very low pulse, chest pain or fainting: stop activity and contact the flight surgeon.

INDS.name: Blood pressure (systolic)
INDS.why: Blood pressure changes with fluid shifts, dehydration and stress. Low pressure also signals orthostatic problems.
how: Sit quietly for 5 minutes, arm at heart level.
Place the cuff on the upper arm and inflate.
Record the top (systolic) number.
a1: Check hydration and salt intake.
Re-measure after resting.
a2: Very high or very low pressure with dizziness or headache: sit/lie down and contact the flight surgeon.

INDS.name: Blood oxygen (SpO₂)
INDS.why: SpO₂ shows how well oxygen reaches blood. Low values point to poor air, lung problems or infection.
how: Warm your hand and rest for 2 minutes.
Clip the pulse oximeter on the index finger.
Wait for a stable value and record it.
a1: Check cabin O₂ and CO₂ and ventilation.
Breathe slowly and re-measure.
a2: Check cabin air, don breathing equipment if needed, and contact the flight surgeon immediately.

INDS.name: Breathing rate
INDS.why: Fast breathing can be an early sign of high CO₂, stress or lung problems.
how: Sit at rest.
Count breaths (one rise + fall) for 30 s and double.
a1: Check cabin CO₂; rest and re-measure.
a2: Persistent fast breathing or breathlessness: check cabin air and contact the flight surgeon.

INDS.name: Fasting blood glucose
INDS.why: Blood sugar reflects energy balance and stress. Nutrition and routine change in space.
how: Measure after 8 h without eating.
Wash and dry the hand, prick the fingertip with a lancet.
Touch the strip to the blood drop and read the meter.
a1: Review food intake, snacks and exercise.
Re-test next week or if you have symptoms.
a2: Very high/low value: follow the protocol (sugary drink if low), recheck and call the flight surgeon.

INDS.name: Hydration (urine colour)
INDS.why: Thirst is weaker in space. Dark urine means you need more water, which also protects the kidneys.
how: Compare urine with the 1–8 colour chart.
1 = pale straw, 8 = dark amber/brown.
a1: Drink 0.5 L of water now and keep sipping during the day.
Re-check in a few hours.
a2: Very dark urine: drink electrolyte fluid, rest, and inform the medical officer — risk of kidney stones and low blood pressure.

INDS.name: Body mass vs pre-flight
INDS.why: Unplanned weight loss means you are not eating enough for the energy you burn.
how: Use the body-mass measurement device.
Compare with your pre-flight mass: enter the change in %.
a1: Increase calories and protein; keep eating schedule.
Re-weigh next week.
a2: Losing over 5% of body mass: urgent diet plan with the flight surgeon.

INDS.name: Exercise today
INDS.why: Resistive plus aerobic exercise (about 2 h/day on the station) is the main protection for bones, muscles and heart.
how: Add up minutes of resistive (ARED), treadmill and cycle training.
a1: Add a short extra session; prioritise resistive exercise.
Plan tomorrow's sessions ahead.
a2: Exercise nearly skipped: schedule time today — bone and muscle loss accumulates quickly.
Tell the flight surgeon if pain or equipment problems stop you.

INDS.name: Back pain
INDS.why: The spine lengthens in weightlessness, and back pain is the most common complaint in orbit.
how: 0 = no pain, 10 = worst imaginable.
Rate your typical pain over the last day.
a1: Stretch and use back-extension exercises; check sleeping posture.
Re-rate tomorrow.
a2: Severe pain, numbness or weakness: stop heavy exercise and contact the flight surgeon.

INDS.name: Body temperature
INDS.why: Fever is the earliest sign of infection, and the immune system is weaker in space.
how: Use the medical thermometer under the tongue for 1 minute.
Wait 15 min after eating, drinking or exercise.
a1: Rest and drink fluid; re-measure in 1–2 hours.
Isolate from crew if you feel sick.
a2: Fever: isolate, hydrate and contact the flight surgeon for treatment guidance.

INDS.name: Radiation dose rate
INDS.why: Space radiation cannot be seen or felt. The dosimeter shows normal levels and warns about solar particle events.
how: Read the personal dosimeter display.
Enter today's dose rate in mSv/day.
a1: Dose is above normal for this location: check space-weather alerts and limit time outside shielded areas.
a2: Move to the storm shelter or best-shielded area and notify mission control.
Log your accumulated dose with the flight surgeon.
